883.title: Caravaggio's Matthew
883.hook: a painting of the tax collector at his table with light falling through a window
883.howItsDone: The Calling of Saint Matthew still hangs in the Contarelli Chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome, where visitors, pilgrims and parishioners stop to look at it before and after Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Palestrina and polyphony, many lines woven into one prayer. Your line was many voices, one word. Last week was for listening; this week, for looking.

In a side chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi, a church in Rome, visitors stand in front of one painting and ask each other: which one is he? Several men sit around a table in a dim room, in the fashionable clothes of the painter's own day: feathered hats, puffed sleeves, a sword. Coins lie on the table. Two figures have just walked in from the right. One of them lifts his hand and points. A shaft of light cuts across the wall above them. The painter is Caravaggio, and the moment is the calling of Matthew.
screen: `WHICH ONE IS HE?` → `MEN AT A TABLE, COINS.` → `A HAND POINTS.`

segments.voice: The Gospel gives this moment a single verse. Matthew is sitting at the custom house, collecting taxes, and Jesus, passing by, says to him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Follow me." And he gets up and follows. Caravaggio stretches that verse into a whole room. First, the ordinary room. No temple, no clouds, no halo to speak of. Tax collectors were distrusted in the Gospels, and Caravaggio sets them in what looks like a back office in his own Rome. The call walks into the place where people count money. Second, the hand. Jesus's hand reaches toward the table, loose, almost lazy. Viewers often notice that it echoes the hand of Adam in Michelangelo's creation scene in the Sistine Chapel. A call, the painting suggests, is a kind of new creation. Third, the light. It comes from behind Jesus, from the upper right, and runs across the wall in the same direction as his hand. The light points where he points. Fourth, the question. The bearded man at the table gestures, maybe at himself: me? Or maybe at the young man beside him, slumped over the coins, who won't look up. For a long time viewers took the bearded man for Matthew; some art historians now argue it's the young one. The painting doesn't settle it. Either way, in Caravaggio's telling, the call lands on someone who hasn't earned it, sitting with his money in a dim room, and the light gets there first.
screen: `A BACK OFFICE IN ROME.` · `A HAND LIKE ADAM'S.` · `THE LIGHT RUNS WITH THE HAND.` · `ME? OR HIM?` · then, large: `FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: If you can, find a picture of the Calling of Saint Matthew and let your eyes go where the light goes, then to the hand, then to the faces at the table, one by one. Which one do you take for Matthew? If you pray, hear the words follow me as spoken to you; if you don't, keep looking, slowly.
Caravaggio's Matthew. The Calling of Saint Matthew, painted for a chapel in Rome, where light and a pointing hand find a tax collector at his table.
Your line: the light points. Tomorrow, red stone ruins and a forest in South America. See you then.

884.title: The Paraguay missions
884.hook: Jesuits and Guaraní peoples built towns together, which colonial powers later ended
884.howItsDone: Catholics in Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil visit the mission ruins as pilgrims and tourists, and some parishes there still sing and play music from the mission tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caravaggio's Matthew, the tax collector at his table and the light running with Jesus's hand. Your line was the light points. Today, a church of red stone in the forest.

Red sandstone walls stand roofless on a green hill in southern Paraguay. Carved angels play instruments along a frieze, one of them a harp. Grass grows where the floor was. This was once a town's church, with a plaza, rows of houses, workshops, a school, fields around it. The people who built and lived in it were Guaraní. The priests who lived among them were Jesuits. Then the towns were emptied, and the forest came back.
screen: `RED STONE IN THE GRASS.` → `ANGELS WITH HARPS.` → `A TOWN, THEN THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: The Spanish called these towns reducciones, reductions, meaning people gathered together into a settlement. First, the shelter. Colonists wanted Guaraní labor, and slave raiders came from the Portuguese side to carry people off. The Jesuits gathered Guaraní families into towns under the Spanish crown, where settlers had no claim on their work. At one point the Guaraní were even allowed to carry arms to defend themselves. Second, the language. The Jesuits learned Guaraní instead of replacing it. They preached in it, wrote grammars, and printed books in it. Third, the music and the work. The towns had workshops, fields held in common, choirs and orchestras. Guaraní craftsmen built instruments and played European music in the forest. Acts describes the first believers, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul." Fourth, the end. Spain and Portugal redrew their border and ordered Guaraní towns handed over. The Guaraní resisted and were defeated in war. Then the Spanish king expelled the Jesuits from his lands, and the towns slowly emptied. People still argue about the missions. Some see a refuge that protected a people and their language. Others see priests who, however kind, ran the Guaraní's lives for them. The two readings don't cancel each other out. What the stones themselves show is the work of Guaraní builders and carvers, whose hands cut those walls and many of those angels.
screen: `A SHELTER FROM SLAVE RAIDERS.` · `PREACHING IN GUARANÍ.` · `WORKSHOPS, FIELDS AND ORCHESTRAS.` · `A BORDER, A WAR, AN EXPULSION.` · then, large: `ONE HEART AND ONE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Look at your own hands for a moment, then think of the hands that cut that red stone and carved those angels. Bring to mind Guaraní families today, in Paraguay and its neighbors, speaking a language their ancestors kept alive. If you pray, pray for them, their land and their children; if you don't, hold them in mind with respect.
Reducción. The Spanish word for a settlement where Guaraní families were gathered together, under Jesuit priests, sheltered from slave raiders.
Your line: the reductions. The red stone still stands where the towns once were. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

885.title: Paul of the Cross (1694–1775)
885.hook: he founds the Passionists to remember Christ's passion
885.howItsDone: Passionist priests, brothers and nuns wear the sign of the Passion on their habits and still preach parish missions and lead retreats centered on the cross, and Catholics often pray before a crucifix, especially on Fridays and in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paraguay missions, the reducción towns of red stone and carved angels. Your line was the reductions. Today, a preacher who carried one thing everywhere he went.

Sewn on the chest of a black habit is a badge shaped like a heart, with a small cross rising from its top. Inside the heart, in Latin, the words: the Passion of Jesus Christ. The men and women who wear it today are called Passionists. The badge goes back to an Italian man from a merchant family, who said he saw himself dressed this way in prayer, before any such habit existed. He went on to preach in Italian villages, carrying a crucifix. His name in religion was Paul of the Cross.
screen: `A BLACK HABIT.` → `A HEART WITH A CROSS.` → `THE PASSION OF JESUS CHRIST.`

segments.voice: First, the call. As a young man, Paolo Danei felt drawn to a life of prayer and penance. Tradition says that in prayer he saw the black habit and the sign of the Passion, and understood that he was to gather companions who would wear it. He went on retreat and wrote a rule for them. Second, the companions. It was slow; few joined at first. His own brother, John Baptist, stayed beside him. They lived simply on a mountain on the coast of Tuscany, praying and fasting, and the community grew, eventually with nuns as well. Third, the preaching. Passionists went out to farm towns and villages to preach missions: days of sermons, confession and prayer. Paul preached holding a crucifix, telling people about Christ's sufferings as a sign of how much God loved them. Passionists take a special vow to keep the memory of the Passion alive. Fourth, the darkness. His letters show that for long years his own prayer felt dry and empty, as if God were far away. He kept preaching the cross while carrying one inside. He died in Rome, and the Church canonized him. In the letter to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims, Saint Paul the apostle writes: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul of the Cross made that sentence his life's work.
screen: `A HABIT SEEN IN PRAYER.` · `SLOW YEARS, A BROTHER BESIDE HIM.` · `PREACHING WITH A CRUCIFIX.` · `HIS OWN LONG DARKNESS.` · then, large: `SAVE IN THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Hold a crucifix or a cross if one is nearby, or look at a picture of one, and don't study it; just stay with it, the way Paul stayed through his dry years. Bring to mind one person who is suffering, and let the cross and that person rest together; Paul of the Cross believed love could be seen here. If you pray, stay there with Christ in silence and bring that person with you; if you don't, let the image show you what someone gave for others.
Paolo Danei. The birth name of Paul of the Cross, who saw himself in prayer wearing a black habit with the sign of the Passion, before it existed.
Your line: remember the passion. He preached the cross through years when his own prayer felt empty. Rest well.

886.title: Always in need of renewal
886.hook: Vatican II says Christ calls the Church to continual reformation (Unitatis Redintegratio 6)
886.howItsDone: Catholics speak of continual conversion, renewed through confession, Lent and retreats, and parishes and dioceses hold synods and renewal programs to examine how they live the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul of the Cross, born Paolo Danei, preaching the crucifix through his own long darkness. Your line was remember the passion. Today closes a whole stretch of the long story: reform, mission and revolution.

Scaffolding climbs one tower of an old cathedral while Mass goes on inside. Stonemasons up top replace what the weather wore away; a choir below sings what it has sung for generations. The scaffolding doesn't mean the building is false. It means the building is still in use. At the Second Vatican Council, the bishops wrote a sentence about the Church that sounds like that scaffolding. It's in a document on Christian unity, and it says the Church is always being called to renewal.
screen: `SCAFFOLDING ON THE TOWER.` → `MASS GOES ON INSIDE.` → `A SENTENCE FROM THE COUNCIL.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the sentence says this: Christ calls the Church, still on her journey, to keep reforming, and she always needs it, because she is also a human institution on earth. Take it a piece at a time. First, who calls. The council doesn't say reform is a good idea people had. It says the call comes from Christ. Second, what needs renewing. The passage names failings in conduct, in church discipline, even in the way teaching has been worded, and says these should be set right, while keeping distinct the faith itself, which it does not treat as up for change. Third, the road of these past weeks held both. A wounded soldier praying in Manresa, Teresa on the road, Vincent de Paul and the poor, Kongo's king, Mother Seton's schools, the hidden families of Japan. And Galileo, the slave trade, the pain of the California missions, the Jesuits suppressed. Renewal and failure, side by side, in the same Church. Fourth, the person. Catholic teaching speaks of conversion not as something done once, but as a lifelong task for every baptized person. What is true of the Church is true of each member. In the Apocalypse, also called Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims, the one on the throne says: "Behold, I make all things new." Not once and finished. Being made new.
screen: `THE CALL COMES FROM CHRIST.` · `CONDUCT, DISCIPLINE, WORDING.` · `RENEWAL AND FAILURE, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `CONVERSION IS A LIFELONG TASK.` · then, large: `BEHOLD, I MAKE ALL THINGS NEW.`

segments.voice: Think of one habit, one relationship, one corner of your life that has worn down, the way stone wears in weather; not everything, just one. Don't tear it down in your head; ask what a small repair would look like: an apology, a return to something you dropped, a kinder way of speaking. If you pray, ask God for help with it; if you don't, simply hold it honestly.
Perennis reformatio. Latin for continual reformation, the council's phrase for how Christ keeps calling the Church, and every member of it, to be made new.
Your line: always renewing. Tomorrow, the modern Church begins, with a struggling parish priest in a French village. That's day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: The Curé of Ars (1786–1859)
887.hook: a struggling student priest who, his biographers say, came to spend up to sixteen hours a day hearing confessions
887.howItsDone: Catholics go to confession, the sacrament of penance, at their parish, often on Saturdays or before Mass; many parishes add extra hours in Lent and Advent, and priests keep the Curé of Ars's feast on August 4.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Church always being called to renewal, perennis reformatio. Your line was always renewing. Today, the modern Church begins, with a village priest.

A seminary student in France cannot get the Latin to stay in his head. Lectures and exams are all in Latin. He is older than the others, a farmer's son, and he fails. A local priest takes him on as a private pupil and keeps him going, more out of trust than results. Ordained at last, he is sent to a small, quiet village called Ars. His biographers remember the vicar general telling him there was not much love of God in that parish, and that he would put some there. Within his lifetime, people came from far away and waited hours, sometimes days. Not for his Latin: to kneel in a small wooden box and talk to him.
screen: `A STUDENT WHO FAILS THE LATIN.` → `SENT TO A SMALL VILLAGE.` → `CROWDS COME TO ARS.`

segments.voice: His name was Jean-Marie Vianney, and Catholics know him as the Curé of Ars; curé is French for a parish priest. First, the slow start. He was no scholar, and he knew it. What he had was stubbornness and prayer. He spent long hours in his church, and went house to house to know the village's farm families. Second, the box. The confessional is where a Catholic tells a priest their sins and hears the words of absolution, forgiveness given in God's name. His early biographers say that in his later years he sat there up to sixteen hours a day. Tradition says he slept little and ate plainly to keep going. People came because, they said, he listened, and seemed to understand them. Third, a farmer in the back pew. As the story goes, an old man sat in the church for long stretches without moving his lips. Asked what he did there, he answered that he looked at God and God looked at him. The Curé loved that answer, and repeated it. Fourth, why it matters. The Church later named him patron of parish priests. Not brilliant ones; ordinary ones in ordinary places. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells of a shepherd who leaves the flock to find one lost sheep, and says there shall be joy in heaven "upon one sinner that doth penance." One. The Curé of Ars spent his life on the one in front of him.
screen: `A SLOW START, A STUBBORN PRAYER.` · `THE BOX: SIXTEEN HOURS A DAY.` · `I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.` · `PATRON OF ORDINARY PRIESTS.` · then, large: `UPON ONE SINNER THAT DOTH PENANCE.`

segments.voice: Many Catholics take a day like this as a nudge toward confession; whatever your path, let one thing surface that you'd rather not look at, a word said, a thing left undone, and name it quietly to yourself. If you pray, bring that one thing to God; if you don't, let it be seen, and breathe out.

888.title: Pauline Jaricot (1799–1862)
888.hook: a young laywoman in Lyon organizes small groups that fund missions far beyond France
888.howItsDone: Catholic parishes hold a yearly collection for the missions, World Mission Sunday, which supports the Society for the Propagation of the Faith; some Catholics also give a small amount each month through mission societies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Curé of Ars, Jean-Marie Vianney, the village priest in the confessional. Your line was sixteen hours a day. Today, a young woman and a coin.

Lyon, France, a city of silk. In the workshops, women and girls stand at the looms for long days and small pay. One young woman from a well-off family of silk merchants has had a change of heart and put away her fine dresses. Her brother, studying for the priesthood, writes home about missionaries far away and how little they have. She can't send much herself. But she has an idea about the women at the looms. Not one big gift from one rich person. Something tiny, from many hands, every week.
screen: `A CITY OF SILK AND LOOMS.` → `MISSIONARIES WITH LITTLE.` → `SOMETHING TINY, EVERY WEEK.`

segments.voice: Her name was Pauline Jaricot. She was not a nun, and never became one; she stayed a laywoman her whole life. First, the circle. She asked a small group of friends and workers to give a small coin each week, and to pray for the missions. Each of them gathered a small group of their own. Groups fed into groups. Second, the network. Out of this work came the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, which Catholics still support today when a collection is taken up for the missions. Third, the smallest coin. In Mark's Gospel, Jesus watches a poor widow drop two tiny coins into the temple treasury, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury." In the Latin of the Vulgate, her two coins are duo minuta. Pauline couldn't cross the ocean; neither could the women at the looms. But a small coin, given again and again, could. Fourth, the hard ending. Later in life she put money into a venture meant to give workers decent jobs and a decent life. It failed. People she trusted let her down, and she died in debt and poverty. The Church did not forget her; it later declared her blessed. Her story asks what a small group of ordinary people can do, if each gives a little and keeps giving. Her answer reached far beyond Lyon, though she never saw the places those coins went.
screen: `A COIN A WEEK, AND A PRAYER.` · `CIRCLES BECOME A SOCIETY.` · `THE WIDOW'S TWO COINS.` · `A FAILED VENTURE, A POOR DEATH.` · then, large: `SMALL GROUPS, WHOLE WORLD.`

889.title: John Henry Newman (1801–1890)
889.hook: an Oxford Anglican priest becomes Catholic, and the Church later names him a saint
889.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint John Henry Newman's feast on October 9, and his poem Lead, Kindly Light is sung as a hymn in Catholic and Anglican churches and at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauline Jaricot and her circles of givers. Your line was small groups, whole world. Today, a man on a becalmed ship, and the end of a week.

A sailing ship, stuck. No wind. The sea is flat, and the boat goes nowhere. On board is a young English clergyman who has nearly died of a fever in Sicily. He badly wants to be home; he believes there is work waiting for him there, though he cannot see what it is. So he writes a short poem. It begins with three words, and asks for very little: not a map, not the whole road, just enough light for the next step. People still sing it as a hymn.
screen: `A SHIP WITH NO WIND.` → `FAR FROM HOME, AND ILL.` → `A SHORT POEM ON BOARD.`

segments.voice: The clergyman was John Henry Newman. First, Oxford. Newman was a priest of the Church of England, a fellow of an Oxford college and a preacher at the university church, and his sermons drew students in. He and his friends set out to recover the Church of England's roots in the early Church, and he read the early Christian writers closely. Second, the turn. The deeper he read, the more convinced he became that the Catholic Church was the Church of those early writers. He was received into it. It cost him his post, his place at Oxford and many old friendships, and he wrote that it felt like coming into port after a rough sea. Third, the poem from the ship, written years before his conversion: "Lead, Kindly Light, amid the encircling gloom, Lead Thou me on! The night is dark, and I am far from home; Lead Thou me on!" And the line people remember: "Keep Thou my feet; I do not ask to see The distant scene; one step enough for me." Fourth, the saint. Newman spent his Catholic years as a priest of the Oratory in Birmingham, writing, teaching and looking after a parish, and late in life the pope made him a cardinal. The Church has since canonized him. Anglicans honor him too, and both still sing his poem. The man who asked for one step got a long road, one step at a time.
screen: `AN OXFORD PREACHER.` · `RECEIVED INTO THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.` · `ONE STEP ENOUGH FOR ME.` · `A PRIEST, A CARDINAL, A SAINT.` · then, large: `LEAD, KINDLY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing in your life where you can't see the distant scene, a decision, a worry, a road with no map, and don't try to solve it; ask only for the next step. If you pray, say Newman's words slowly: lead, kindly light, lead thou me on. If you don't, just hold the phrase one step enough.
